item.title: Signs of a highly sensitive person
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Do you cry at paintings and recoil from crowds? A psychologist explores the telltale signs of a ‘highly sensitive person’

- Video by Dr Julie

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: Do paintings make you cry, and do dance clubs make you recoil? You might just be a highly sensitive person (HSP). According to the pioneering research of the US clinical psychologist and author Elaine Aron, some 15 to 20 per cent of the population are highly sensitive people (more recent research puts the figure higher still). This means that, possessing a sensitive nervous system, such people find themselves more attuned to, and sometimes overwhelmed by, physical and emotional stimuli. In this short video, the British clinical psychologist Julie Smith (aka Dr Julie) draws from Aron’s decades of research, including her book The Highly Sensitive Person (1996), to explore some of the telltale signs that you might be an HSP and offer simple advice for flourishing if you have these traits. For a deeper dive into how to thrive as a highly sensitive person, read this Psyche Guide.

item.title: The way we talk to bots matters even if they aren’t conscious
item.dc:creator: HennyGe Wichers
item.description:
If more and more of our daily interactions are ungracious exchanges with machines, we should expect it to change us

- by HennyGe Wichers

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I’m standing in the pouring rain trying to retrieve a parcel from a locker wall that just won’t open. I call the help desk and am greeted by Matt, a customer service chatbot. To get my parcel, I must follow his instructions, describing the problem and speaking in full sentences. But it’s not working, so I ask for a human. Matt asks for my phone number. I give it to him. He says ‘Thank you’ and asks how he can help, again. Minutes pass. The rain is unrelenting, as is the bot’s cheeriness. When the locker finally clicks open, I hang up while he’s still speaking.

A week later, I find myself still thinking about that exchange – about my irritation, and about hanging up on him like that. My discomfort about how I treated the bot might not be unusual. In 2003, the media researchers Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass documented what they called the ‘media equation’: people apply genuine social reflexes to computers automatically, even when we know they aren’t conscious. Some of us say ‘Please’ and ‘Thank you’ to chatbots or feel sorry for robot vacuum cleaners. The researchers’ explanation is not that we’re naive, exactly. Our brains process a voice – any voice – as a social presence, triggering social responses before conscious thought has had a chance to intervene.

But this social reflex isn’t always kind. When people talk to chatbots, we often seem to strip basic courtesy out of the exchange. Our messages become shorter, simpler and more profane, and in one analysis, more than half of conversations included at least one form of insult or verbal aggression.

Chatbots are increasingly woven into daily life, which means that many of us are likely having these automatic – and frequently brusque – social responses multiple times a day. They are becoming habitual. Habits take root, after all, when a behaviour is repeated in stable contexts and driven by consistent cues. You can see this with other ways of using technology: if you pick up your phone to check a message, only to lose yourself for 10 minutes as you scroll your favourite apps, you probably didn’t deliberate about whether to use those apps; you just did it, because that’s what you usually do when you look at your phone. You’ve developed a habit.

Chatbot interactions are, for habit formation, close to ideal. When you have a question and open an AI-based chatbot app, there is little friction or waiting. Often the reward is nearly instantaneous. The register that many of us use when we get there – direct, brief, transactional – is already familiar from voice assistants: instructing Siri to set a timer, commanding ‘Alexa, stop!’ when the smart speaker gets it wrong. The little chatbot prompt box invites the same: cut the fluff and demand what you need. It seems to get results, too. Some studies on prompt tone suggest the systems themselves often respond better to it. And when the machine fails or frustrates the user, the user gets irritated, or even abandons the conversation mid-sentence, as I did.

For me, and for those who’ve been studying how we relate to artificial beings, it’s hard not to wonder if this increasingly normal mode of interacting will change what we’re like in the rest of our lives.

In a study published last year, the sociologists Ashley Harrell and Margaret Traeger tested whether people’s interactions with artificial agents might spill over into those they have with humans. They conducted two experiments with more than 4,000 participants. In each study, the participants played a simple online cooperation game with what they thought was either a bot or another human being (in reality, these other players were all programmed). After 10 rounds, the participants were paired with a new partner – this time, a real human they had never interacted with before – and played again.

People were more instrumental and demanding toward an AI chatbot than another human

A couple of things emerged from the data. The bot’s behaviour mattered: if participants first interacted with an uncooperative bot, they were less cooperative themselves with the human who followed it, compared with participants who started with a cooperative bot. More to the point, participants who began the game with a bot partner were less cooperative afterward than those who started with a human. The researchers traced this to empathy: people felt less empathy towards a bot partner (less compassion, less curiosity about their point of view), and that didn’t immediately reset when a human partner took the bot’s place. The empathy dial, once it was turned down, stayed down.

The bots in this study were simple: just a programmed image on a screen, not a conversational AI. Yet the effects still showed. In another experiment with an AI chatbot, people who briefly collaborated with a bot were more instrumental and demanding toward their collaborator compared with those who thought they were working with another human – and they later judged other people’s work more harshly. What immersive chatbot systems might do, over time, to how people treat each other is still hard to know, but these are early signs of how spillover can happen. As we contemplate where it goes from here, a different kind of thinking could be helpful.

The ethicist Tae Wan Kim at Carnegie Mellon University has spent years thinking about what we owe to robots and what we owe to ourselves – two things that he considers inseparable. Kim draws on the Confucian concept li, which translates roughly as ‘rite’ or ‘ritual’. In Confucian thought, li refers not only to formal ceremonies but also to everyday forms of interaction such as a greeting or a gesture of gratitude. The philosopher Herbert Fingarette described what this looks like in practice in Confucius: The Secular as Sacred (1972): two people meet on the street, one extends a hand, and the other turns, smiles, reaches out – a moment of ‘spontaneous and perfect cooperative action’ so habitual that people barely notice it. That unremarkable exchange, Kim and his co-author Alan Strudler write, is li. And it matters, because each time someone does it, they become slightly more the kind of person who does it.

As Kim told me, li ‘includes countless everyday routines and forms of speech, and it treats participation in proper ritual as something that shapes people into more civil, mutually respectful agents.’ Exchanges with an AI are becoming another kind of everyday interaction, and, seen this way, every message we send is practice for the kind of people we become.

This takes us beyond the obvious argument that it doesn’t matter how we treat bots because, unlike another person or animal, bots can’t be harmed. The question of how we should treat a dog or a chimpanzee is a question about the animal. With chatbots, the question is about how the ill-treatment affects the human. Kim’s point, and what the cooperation-game research suggests, is that something is at stake for us. If we develop a habit of talking to chatbots in an instrumental, impatient and dismissive register, we are rehearsing a way of interacting with others.

Technology has always shaped the social norms and expectations of its time, often in ways that are noticed only in retrospect. Cinema set standards for romantic love, ones that real life rarely measures up to. The internet made it easier to meet people – and to avoid them. Social media changed the way many of us present ourselves to the world and how we feel about our own lives. These effects followed from specific design choices, business incentives and the habits people settled into. Chatbots are the latest instance in this pattern.

The instrumental register suits the companies building these systems just fine: short exchanges are convenient for users and cheaper for AI companies to process and, in this business, greater efficiency means greater profits. That’s one reason the tone could readily spread. Many millions of people are now regularly using chatbots and rehearsing it.

Enough people rehearsing the same instrumental register multiple times a day could influence what ordinary conversation sounds like

The sociologist Erving Goffman used the term ‘interaction order’ to describe the unwritten rules that govern how people behave with each other in everyday life. This includes things like when to speak and pause, how much warmth and patience to show. These rules of everyday interaction can feel so natural we don’t realise they exist until they start to change.

Think of how potentially awkward conversations are often moved to text or email, or how read receipts have imbued a recipient’s silence with meaning. Nobody decided one day that that’s the way things would be. It just came to be part of how many people interact. The concern here is similar: that enough people rehearsing the same instrumental register multiple times a day could influence what ordinary conversation sounds like and how much patience we bring to exchanges that don’t go smoothly. What do we carry over to the call-centre worker who can’t fix our problem; the colleague who misunderstands us; the partner who needs us to say it again?

But the direction of change is not necessarily fixed. As Kim put it: ‘chatbot design can also rehearse patience, warmth, and civility.’ One study found that a bot that met abuse with expressions of empathy – rather than avoidance or retaliation – left people feeling less angry and more guilty. A chatbot that pushes back gently or redirects hostility is doing something different from one that is optimised for speed or engagement. The interaction feels different, and it may leave the user slightly different too. The texture of these interactions is, in part, a design choice, one that the people building these systems are making right now. The rest is up to us – a choice we make every time we open the app. We don’t need to pretend the chatbot has feelings. Maybe it’s enough to notice when impatience gets the better of us, and to pause before we let that become our normal way of speaking.

This brings me back to Matt. I still don’t know why I hung up while he was still talking. Irritation, probably. The rain didn’t help. I’m not sure it mattered to anyone but me. But that’s the point: it did matter to me, because of what I was practising, and what I might carry with me.

item.title: The evil eye is irrational. Abandon it at your peril
item.dc:creator: Timna Abramov
item.description:
So many of the world’s superstitions have been supplanted by rational thinking. Why does one of the oldest beliefs persist?

- by Timna Abramov

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
When I was a child, I went to the wedding of a cousin I barely knew. After the sun had set, I watched the newly married couple walk through the crowd and begin to dance together. As they moved, the voices of dozens of guests rung out in a loud, high-pitched trill: lililililili!

Curious, I asked my aunt what they were doing.

‘They’re warding away the evil eye,’ she told me.

She explained that, during happy occasions, like weddings, the loud noise frightened away evil spirits and protected the couple.

As I grew older, I began to notice the other protections my family used against the evil eye. Charms were fastened onto necklaces and bracelets, and the phrase ‘tfu tfu tfu’ would be uttered anytime someone received a compliment. During significant, unpredictable processes – negotiating the price of a car, for example, or attending interviews for a new job – one might even refrain from telling anyone, just in case the evil eye sabotages them. And, of course, wedding ceremonies rang with ululations.

These are just a small handful of the ancient protections that humans have summoned against envy. For envy is the mechanism by which the evil eye operates. It emerges whenever someone looks at another person with resentment and jealousy, even unintentionally. Bad luck then follows, targeting things of value: wealth, health, good jobs and happy marriages.

Eventually, customs against the evil eye became a regular part of my own life. But, to members of cultures that do not subscribe to it, this ancient superstition, passed down over millennia, is often treated with suspicion, and considered incompatible with modern rationality. The contrast between these attitudes prompts the question: should we let go of old familial superstitions in favour of reason?

Belief in the evil eye goes back to the earliest known civilisation: Sumer. Texts written on clay tablets around 5,000 years ago show that the Sumerians believed the evil eye was a destructive power capable of destroying harvests, depleting wealth and causing illness. It could be cast by animals, gods and people – even by accident. One text, The Instructions of Shuruppak, advises: ‘Do not do evil with your eye.’ Other proverbs from this text warn of the danger of envious looks:

Who speaks curses injures only the skin;
Greedy eyes, however, can kill.

A belief in the destructive power of envy would transcend Sumerian superstition. A line from a Mesopotamian poem, composed during the Old Babylonian period roughly 3,600 to 3,900 years ago, makes the connection even more explicit:

He did not flaunt his knowledge. His words were modest.
If he flaunted his knowledge, people would cast the evil eye on him.

Romans decorated their homes with absurd depictions to ward away jealous gazes

This belief – that being looked at with envy or greed could cause harm – persisted as the cultures of the Near East emerged, succeeded one another and spread. Traces of the evil eye can be found in Babylonian incantations, on Phoenician amulets and in the Hebrew Bible. Some of those amulets may even have birthed the modern hamsa charm – a palm-shaped amulet that has become one of the most well-known protections against the evil eye.

By the classical period, starting around 2,800 years ago, the belief was widespread: Socrates cautioned against loud praise lest the evil eye sabotage his argument, while Romans decorated their homes with absurd depictions to ward away jealous gazes. In Pompeii, for example, two freed slaves, who had become rich, decorated their atrium with a comic fresco of the god Priapus weighing his oversized phallus against a sack of coins – an image meant to provoke laughter and ward off the envious looks of visitors. Later, roughly around the years 27-30 CE, the evil eye appeared in Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount. Centuries later, it appeared again in the Islamic Hadiths.

Today, belief in the evil eye exists across the world. In Italy, it is known as malocchio (and countered by phallus-like horn-shaped charms or by touching the crotch). In Greece, it is known as mati. Across Turkey and the Arab world, its name is nazar. Versions of the evil eye are found almost everywhere: North Africa, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, parts of eastern Europe, India, sub-Saharan Africa and southeast Asia – not to mention diaspora and immigrant communities across the globe.

The evil eye may seem like an irrational, pseudoscientific belief. The explanations ancient writers conceived to explain the mechanism by which it worked (or to ward it away) are even less convincing. Plutarch, for example, hypothesised that the eye emitted toxic rays that poisoned its object.

Some ancient thinkers cautioned against this kind of superstition. Plato, Lucretius and Cicero all discouraged superstitious beliefs, citing the anxiety they cause believers. Today, we would identify the excessive distress these thinkers describe as ‘scrupulosity’, a pathological obsession with religious correctness associated with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Their criticism of superstitions could be rather harsh: Theophrastus mocked those who shudder or spit when they see ‘a maniac or an epileptic’ – an expression of what he called ‘cowardice in regard to the supernatural’. (Spitting away the gaze is still practised today and, unfortunately, the idea that the sick and disabled are powerful casters of the evil eye also persists. And the association goes both ways: in a 2014 survey of Jordanian university students, 28.1 per cent believed the evil eye causes epilepsy. This is a potent reminder of superstition’s risks.)

While misfortune is unpredictable, these rituals return the locus of control to the afflicted

Ancient philosophers who cautioned against superstitions did so with good intentions. They were looking out for the spiritual wellbeing of their peers. But their approach still led to patronising views of ‘superstitious’ people, which almost always meant non-Roman cultures. Romans scrutinised and banned Egyptian cultic practice, and mocked Christians and Jews as superstitiosi for observing their rites.

The disapproval of superstition on ethnic and rational grounds reappeared in 19th-century research on the evil eye. Consider the writing of the British anthropologist Edward B Tylor in his book Primitive Culture (1871):

Of course, the opinions and habits belonging in common to masses of mankind are to a great extent the results of sound judgment and practical wisdom. But to a great extent it is not so. That many numerous societies of men should have believed in the influence of the evil eye … is not ground for holding that the rites in question are profitable, the beliefs sound, and the history authentic.

Strange interpretations of the evil eye persisted into the next century. The Hungarian American psychoanalyst and anthropologist Géza Róheim, after observing how common the hamsa was across North Africa, reached the startling conclusion that the hand amulet was rooted in masturbation. As he put it: ‘the use of masturbation as a means of warding off anxiety is well known. I suspect that this is the meaning of the hand amulet.’ Interpretations like this have made it easy to write off a belief in the evil eye as absurd.

Modern attitudes are not far off. A 2024 article in Scientific American, entitled ‘Why Do Superstitions Persist among Seemingly Rational People?’, implies that practising superstitions is incompatible with a rational character.

Having grown up at the intersection of several cultures that believe in the evil eye, I’ve come across many intelligent people who take part in superstitious rituals. There are good reasons why they adopt these seemingly irrational beliefs. From an evolutionary perspective, superstitions are theorised to be a byproduct of the human ability to detect and explain patterns with astounding speed and accuracy. Additionally, the collective rituals we form around superstitions relieve our anxiety in the face of uncontrollable events, such as the weather that once affected harvests in Sumer or the onset of epilepsy in ancient Greece. While misfortune is unpredictable, these rituals return the locus of control to the afflicted. This is likely the mechanism behind the observation that taking part in positive rituals may boost performance, which has been attested to in several studies. Better still, rituals against the evil eye frequently return agency to those who need it most, because it is not priests or princes who have the power to repel the evil eye. In some cultures, the people most credited with the power to ward off the evil eye are those who have traditionally had fewer social and legal rights – old women in the Balkans, disabled people in ancient Greece and Rome.

Being seen can be terrifying. It is the first step to being judged, loathed, and excluded

Moreover, regarding the evil eye with contempt is a missed opportunity to examine why it is so persistent. Given how widespread the belief is, it likely has its social advantages. It can be immensely powerful as a social bonder: because the eye targets precisely what societies hold dearest, it is used across cultures to reinforce and define collective values. Consequently, many enduring evil-eye rituals protect those once seen as most vulnerable: pregnant women, children and newborns. Modern medicine may have made that vulnerability less visible, but the survival of spitting, charms and amulets tied to these life stages keeps us in touch with the anxieties of the past. They also provide perspective. Despite healthcare innovations, life itself cannot be taken for granted. As societies evolve, the scope of coverage provided by rituals widens. In my life, among friends and family, it is customary to murmur protective phrases at the mention of a potential job offer. In doing so, we show each other what our social circle values.

Helpful qualities aside, the belief itself is a rich cultural tradition. Behind the amulets and other items used to ward off the evil eye is a wealth of intangible culture. These items frequently draw on regional variations of the belief. North African Jews, for example, combined hamsa amulets with fish motifs, inspired by the Talmudic teaching that fish, hidden from envious looks underwater, are immune to the evil eye. Each culture preserves variants that tell a unique story.

The greatest criticism levelled against the evil-eye superstition rests on the assumption that the phenomenon is unsubstantiated. In a literal sense, it is. But from a social perspective, being seen can be terrifying. It is the first step to being judged, loathed, and excluded. We feel this intuitively when we worry about appearing too gaudy, too dressed-up, too eye-catching.

In the 20th century, philosophers pondered the power dynamics behind looking and being looked at. Jean-Paul Sartre developed the concept of ‘the look’ (‘le regard’), the realisation that being looked at transforms us from free agents into visible objects. Michel Foucault observed that societies weaponise the power discrepancy between those who are looked at and those who look, such as specialists in medical clinics and guards in prisons. John Berger pointed out that being viewed is rife with tensions, propelled by gender, class and ideology. It is unsurprising, then, that so early in our history, humans concluded that the eye has a special power.

The evil-eye superstition regulates this anxiety and, crucially, the behaviour around it.

One of history’s earliest surviving references to this ancient superstition is, not coincidentally, ‘do not do evil with your eye.’ The belief warns us against boasting, and against envying others, and it asks us to protect ourselves during vulnerable periods, while also worrying for those who are more vulnerable than ourselves. In short, it teaches us a valuable lesson: to look upon others kindly.

item.title: How to cope with the stress of anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice
item.dc:creator: Kiki Fehling
item.description:
A queer psychologist shares skills from dialectical behaviour therapy to help you cope and find joy in a stigmatising world

- by Kiki Fehling

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
‘It’s such a relief to finally be in a room with people who just get it.’ I heard this message a lot when I was providing group therapy sessions for LGBTQ+ clients. The group members on any given day might have included a gay man who’d had slurs blurted at him; a trans woman who worried about how her clothing choices affected her safety; a pansexual woman who painfully doubted her queerness because she was married to a man; or an intersex person who felt broken after hearing yet another politician claim ‘there are only two biological sexes’. Although their identities and experiences differed, there was a connection. A shared understanding of the myriad ways that being LGBTQ+ in today’s world can be stressful.

Indeed, most of my queer clients had experienced some form of LGBTQ+ minority stress – the unique social pressures and emotional burdens that people face due to anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice, bias and discrimination. These clients were also creative and resilient. In that group therapy space, they collaboratively learned how to cope with the anxiety, shame and stress they experienced. As a queer person myself, I learned along with them as they shared.

If you’re queer – ie, a member of the LGBTQ+ community – minority stress could be negatively affecting your mental health, especially if you don’t know how to cope with it. In this Guide, I’ll share some of the wisdom that the group members and I found together in that space.

Why minority stress matters

Compared with heterosexual and cisgender people, LGBTQ+ people face particularly high rates of anxiety, depression and other mental health difficulties. These disparities are not caused by being LGBTQ+. Rather, they’re related to living in a world that stigmatises same-gender attractions, gender-expansive expressions and queer ways of being.

The minority stress model, which advanced this idea scientifically, is supported by decades of research, and queer people can benefit from learning about it. Better understanding what LGBTQ+ stressors are, as well as how they can accumulate and affect you, can help you have more compassion for your own experience.

You may have faced some, or many, of these stressors yourself:

  • Experienced or witnessed discrimination. This includes being mistreated, called names, rejected, harassed or physically assaulted because you are LGBTQ+. Even unintentional or seemingly small instances of discrimination (sometimes called ‘microaggressions’) can negatively impact a queer person’s mental health, as can witnessing other queer people being discriminated against. Living in jurisdictions with anti-LGBTQ+ laws or policies appears to have a negative impact on LGBTQ+ people’s health, too.
  • Anticipated discrimination. Many queer people, because they have experienced or witnessed discrimination in the past, understandably expect to experience it in the future. If this is the case for you, you might also feel on edge in social situations, worry about being hurt or judged, or struggle with rejection sensitivity or hypervigilance.
  • Concealment. To protect themselves from discrimination, many queer people choose to hide or deny their LGBTQ+ identity. This might include actively changing the way you talk, dress or act in order to appear straight, cisgender or somehow ‘less queer’. While concealment may help a person avoid harm or rejection, it’s cognitively taxing and might lead to its own psychological problems.
  • Internalised stigma and shame. Many modern cultures are packed with stigmatising messages that being LGBTQ+ is wrong, sick, weird or bad in some way. If you hear these messages enough times, you might start to believe them. These internalised negative beliefs can lead to you to judge yourself, other queer people or specific ‘queer’ ways of being. They can also contribute to chronic shame or self-doubt.

Of course, if you have more than one marginalised identity – eg, if you are also a person of colour, have a disability, or you’re a woman or a femme person – you’ve likely experienced unique and intersectional forms of these stressors.

Experiencing minority stress does not doom LGBTQ+ people to perpetual mental health struggles. Many are mentally healthy and thriving, and research shows that numerous things can help protect queer people’s wellbeing. One such protective factor is learning coping skills, like the ones taught in dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). While DBT was originally created to treat people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, it teaches dozens of skills that have been shown to help reduce anxiety, depression, substance use and other mental health difficulties. It also can be helpful for LGBTQ+ people specifically.

Knowing how to deal with minority stress and painful emotions – as well as how to more fully connect with queer joy and other pleasant emotions – is essential for queer mental health. What follows are some specific, practical tools and ideas to help you deal with the stressful experiences that LGBTQ+ people face today.

item.title: What does it mean to have relationship ambivalence?
item.dc:creator: Francesca Righetti
item.description:
When a relationship provokes both strong positive and negative feelings in you, it can take a toll – here’s what’s going on

- by Francesca Righetti

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
We tend to talk about our relationships as either satisfying or unsatisfying, healthy or toxic. This either/or perspective shapes a lot of relationship advice, and filters through to the ways many of us chat about our relationship dilemmas with friends. But the reality is that many of our most consequential relationships in life are both positive and negative at the same time (or neither positive nor negative – which I’ll come back to later).

You can love your partner tremendously and hate their lack of responsibility. You can feel deeply grateful to your in-laws for all the support they offer while at the same time feeling extremely annoyed by their intrusiveness. You can admire your boss’s effectiveness and be irritated by their micromanaging.

My colleagues and I recently put forward a new four-quadrant framework for how people evaluate their relationships. The experiences I just described would fall into the ambivalent quadrant, which is characterised by having both strong positive and negative feelings toward another person at the same time. The other quadrants are feeling mostly positive, mostly negative or indifferent. We believe that ambivalence in relationships has been largely overlooked up until now, even though it’s such a common and consequential experience.

It’s important to say that being in an ambivalent relationship is not the same as finding it mildly satisfying – the distinctive nature of these relationships is that you experience strong positive feelings and strong negative feelings. It’s also important to distinguish ambivalence from indifference, which occurs when neither positive nor negative feelings are strong and the relationship instead feels emotionally neutral. In other words, ambivalence is ‘I care a lot, but I’m torn,’ while indifference is closer to ‘I’m not especially drawn in, upset, or emotionally invested.’

How does ambivalence arise in relationships? Certainly, some relationships are a mixed package from their very beginning: offering great warmth and connection alongside quirks, costs or complications that never quite disappear. Since their start, they stir both gratitude and frustration, attraction and hesitation. But ambivalence can also grow over time. Relationships evolve and studies show that even relationships that start out mostly positive (such as romantic relationships) often accumulate negative feelings as life unfolds and significant challenges emerge. Partners change, circumstances shift, responsibilities grow heavier. What once felt effortless now involves compromises, mismatched needs or recurring patterns we didn’t see in the early glow. When these negative feelings first emerge, the positive ones do not suddenly dissipate, thus creating ambivalence.

Think about a relationship in your own life that leaves you feeling torn. Maybe you care deeply about this person and value the bond, yet also feel hurt, frustrated or disappointed by them. If that feels unsettling, our findings suggest there is a reason: people are often distressed by the mixed feelings of relationship ambivalence. We do not want to feel pulled in opposite directions about someone who matters to us. In fact, our studies (and research by others) have shown that ambivalence in romantic relationships undermines both relationship quality and personal wellbeing. And the strain is not only psychological: experiencing ambivalence has been linked to higher blood pressure, greater inflammation and other early markers of cardiovascular risk.

Uncertainty doesn’t just chip away at relationship quality, it also affects wellbeing

Despite this tension, we’ve found that ambivalence doesn’t tend to mean that people check out of a relationship – if anything, it often means the opposite. When someone feels both pulled in and pushed away, they tend to stay mentally busy trying to ‘solve’ the ambivalence: they want to either like or dislike someone; they want to figure out whether the relationship is worth investment or whether it is best to pull away. In fact, in our studies we found that the more ambivalence someone experiences in a romantic relationship, the more they think and ruminate about it.

These ruminative thoughts tend to swing in two directions. At times they are constructive and people think about ways to improve things, fix patterns, reconnect. Other times, their thoughts are pretty destructive, focusing on all the difficulties, problems and flaws of the relationships. That same push‑pull shows up in behaviour. Some days people act warmly and constructively, trying to connect with the other person. On other days, people are destructive, by withdrawing or blaming and criticising others. And in our studies that have tracked people over time, we see that ambivalence reliably produces these swings, making people fluctuate substantially between these two different types of thoughts and behaviours on a daily basis.

So feeling ambivalent does not seem like a walk in the woods. It is stressful and consequential for how people behave in their relationship. And what about the person on the receiving end? What happens when your partner has both strong positive and strong negative feelings toward you: one day they want to connect, the next they pull back or critique, and the cycle repeats? Being on the receiving end of those mixed signals can feel destabilising. And those shifts – from connection to distance, from support to irritation – aren’t just confusing; they can take a toll on the sense of safety and stability in the relationship. In fact, in our studies, we find that recipients of ambivalence often experience their partner as unpredictable and hard to read. That uncertainty doesn’t just chip away at relationship quality, it also affects the wellbeing of the recipient of the ambivalence. Recipients report feeling more stressed, in a more negative mood, and less satisfied with their lives overall. It’s clear that ambivalence isn’t a solo experience, it tends to spill over, influencing (and potentially damaging) the person on the other side of the relationship, too.

If you recognise these descriptions of relationship ambivalence including the challenges involved, you might be wondering if there’s anything you can do about it. There’s no quick fix, but there is some good news. First, ambivalence means that the relationship matters to you. Mixed feelings – strong positives and strong negatives – show up only when someone is important to us. If the relationship didn’t matter to you, you wouldn’t feel torn; you would feel indifferent. Indifference is the state where even the negative feelings have faded – you’re no longer frustrated or hurt, you’ve simply stopped noticing. So ambivalence, uncomfortable as it is, signals that this is still a meaningful relationship. Second, ambivalence makes you reflect on the relationship. You are involved, you want to understand what is going on, and decide what should happen next. Ambivalence is an important signal that shows you that a rewarding and valuable relationship poses significant costs too, nudging you to ask whether to repair, recalibrate or step back.

All this means that if you are now recognising for the first time that a significant relationship in your life is ambivalent for you, this awareness is already an important first step. Becoming aware of your mixed feelings creates an opportunity to reflect on the relationship.

This is a good moment to intervene and influence what happens next. After all, if you are having these mixed feelings, it means two helpful conditions are present:

  1. There’s still some positivity to build on. The relationship has rewards; the task is to reduce the negativity, not to build positivity from scratch; and
  2. You are still engaged. You care, you’re motivated, and you’re open to making things better – whether through conversation, reflection, counselling or other forms of support (in other words, you are not in the indifferent quadrant of our framework, which would be worse news for the relationship!)

If negativity comes to overwhelm the positives – or if you find yourself starting to drift into indifference – then your window for change will have narrowed. Ambivalence, in contrast, sits in a workable in‑between zone, where effort still has room to make a difference. It can be a moment to approach the other person, communicate your needs, and see whether you can find ways together that allow the relationship to improve. After all, ambivalence is the emotional equivalent of a blinking yellow light: not a stop, not a go, but an invitation to pay attention. And with the right attention, many relationships can still find their better path.

item.title: Lesser choices
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Estelle recalls being blindfolded and fearful in Mexico City – a timely vision of a world without abortion rights

- Directed by Courtney Stephens

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
In Lesser Choices (2022), the Los Angeles-based filmmaker Courtney Stephens interviews her mother, Estelle, as she recalls the experience of seeking an abortion in 1969. This was before the US Supreme Court’s decision in Roe v Wade established a constitutional right to abortion in 1973 and, of course, well before that decision was overturned in 2022. Like many women at the time, Estelle found her answer in a clandestine provider in Mexico City – a process that, to her, proved that she was ‘willing to do anything to not be pregnant’.

Stephens pairs the interview audio with Super 8 images of Mexico City, building a tension between the nostalgic, home-movie aesthetic and the traumatic memories recounted in their conversation. In doing so, she reveals two contrasting truths in her mother’s story: her fear of the process itself, and the freedom she found in choosing when, and on what terms, to grow her family. For more from Stephens, watch her short Ida Western Exile.

item.title: The softness of metal
item.dc:creator: Keith Kahn-Harris
item.description:
Watching a seated Ozzy play his final gig, my ankle broken, I’m in tears – this couldn’t be more metal

- by Keith Kahn-Harris

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I am grateful no one else is in the room with me. In principle, I’ve no problem with my family seeing me cry: but blinking away hot salty tears while watching Ozzy Osbourne? That seems somehow ludicrous. This is, after all, the self-styled prince of darkness, a trickster-like figure – one part devil, one part joker, one part joke.

I thought I knew Ozzy – we all thought we knew him, whether we liked him or not. He was the fresh-faced, charismatic vocalist of Black Sabbath. He was the bloated, crazed, drug-addled artist who bit the head off a dead bat onstage and once tried to strangle his wife. Later in life he was the lovable, bewildered paterfamilias on The Osbournes reality TV series. For some, he was also the artist with a back catalogue on which much of metal still rests.

The Ozzy that is making me cry is none of those things.

Here I am, in the easy chair in our living room, laptop balanced on my thighs, my recently broken ankle encased in a support boot and raised up on a bolster. Weeping. My lower leg and foot prickle with heat on this sultry day in July 2025, and I cannot take my eyes off Ozzy performing the final show of his illustrious career, at Villa Park in Birmingham, UK, before an ecstatic audience, and for those like me who have paid for the live stream. There are no antics, no wide-eyed devilish grin, none of the incessant running back and forth that we’re used to from him. Instead, he sits on a bat-shaped throne, singing with an appalling intensity, and occasionally demanding that the crowd clap along.

All day long I’d been watching metal’s great and good perform brief sets in honour of the man who inspired so many of them. Grizzled veteran megastars like Metallica, emerging legends like Gojira and fresh-faced talents like Yungblud and Lzzy Hale – all of them merely support acts just for one day, playing brief sets in which Ozzy/Sabbath covers predominate. Now, finally, it’s Ozzy’s turn.

He had been waiting for this moment to say a final goodbye for years. Health problems and the COVID-19 pandemic meant he’d had to cancel most of his farewell tour. Three years on from his only stage appearance since then (a couple of songs performed at a 2022 NFL game), he is obliged to perform seated due to a litany of medical complaints: Parkinson’s disease, acute back and neck trouble, and a whole lot else. You can see that singing takes everything he has left. He wants to stand, to run, to be the embodiment of rock and roll that he once was. It’s heartbreaking.

Ozzy professes his love for us and we return it, myself included. Even viewed on a laptop screen from my own sick chair, it feels like a deluge of emotion. A surfeit of love, pain, frailty and loss are converging on my own frail body.

When I first discovered Ozzy and metal, as a child on the cusp of adolescence, metal bodies seemed like the embodiment of strength and virility. The tousled locks, the phallic guitar poses, the distortion, the screams and the implausible vibrato – all this felt like what a man should be. Metal bodies thrilled me, the more so since, as a skinny, nebbish Jew, I felt I could never inhabit one.

He was always different, pudgy, vulnerable, a ball of emotion and confusion

My Jewish North London upbringing was settled, middle class, rule bound. Metal was none of those things and nor was Ozzy. Metal was confrontation, insensitive and insouciant to the loathing and derision its artists received from the mainstream music majority. Ozzy lived a life wilfully devoted to the pursuit of shock. His music, and metal more generally, explored the darkest of themes; violence, death and suicide, the occult, all the delights of transgression.

Yet, had I looked a little deeper, I would have discovered a different Ozzy that coexisted with the one I knew; an Ozzy I might have found common ground with. Physically, he was never a metal god either. He was always different, pudgy, vulnerable, a ball of emotion and confusion, far from the image of masculine mastery. Like me, he desperately felt he had to embody metal. Like me, he frequently felt shame for the weakness of his flesh. Unlike me, he somehow became the apotheosis of metal masculinity.

I spend the week before the show suffering, after slipping down the stairs in the middle of the night. It was my daughter’s Father’s Day card that I slipped on – a metaphor I don’t even want to think about. After a couple of days hobbling around the house, I give in to reality and get an X-ray. While I am waiting for the results, my son calls to tell me he was awarded a first class in his honours degree. I yelp. Then I learn that my ankle is fractured.

I spend the day before Ozzy’s final show alternately being wheeled and limping around a university town for the ceremonial awarding of my son’s degree. It’s a luminous, barely believable day, as I remember my son’s late diagnosis of dyslexia and the educational turmoil he’d had to cope with during the pandemic.

Ozzy’s brave performance stirs an emotional pot already full to the brim

In the afterglow of these hours spent marinating in love, and as I watch Ozzy declaring his love for the crowd, I can’t entirely banish the undercurrent of guilt that never leaves me on account of another bond of love: my immobility means that I haven’t been to visit my father today, in the nursing home where he has been confined for nearly a year. Like Ozzy, my dad has Parkinson’s disease and much else; standing up is a chancy enterprise for him. This week he won’t receive the fleeting comfort of a visit from me. It was my turn to be the man, to take over from the one who once carried me. Instead, there is only my weakness.

A weak father, a weak son; immobile while watching a weak man somehow transcend his desperate situation. So I cry, as Ozzy’s brave performance stirs an emotional pot already full to the brim.

I’ve spent years studying metal as a scholar and writing about it anywhere that will publish me. I know that metal today is a more diverse place. London’s best metal pub has a vegan menu and its best metal record store has an alcohol-free bar; metal festivals have viewing platforms for people with mobility issues. Metal is even used as a resource in support groups and 12-step programmes. Yet Ozzy’s performance still shocks me into a different kind of understanding. Who knew that metal could be a place where one of its most notorious stars could perform this achingly sad display of vulnerability and yearning?

Confined to his throne-cum-prison, Ozzy clearly feels something of this unnerving surprise himself. You can tell that his frustration with his disability is tinged with a portion of shame. He loves the love he’s getting, but he can’t play the transgressive part he’s played for so long. The pathos of his evident grief, his mourning the loss of what he once was, is hard to witness.

What appears to be metallic hardness is but a patina for something else

Ozzy may have helped create heavy metal but that doesn’t mean that he fully understood his creation, its possibilities and potential. Then again, for much of metal’s history, neither did anyone else. We were all sucked into the myth that the metal men were selling, to the point where we sometimes forgot that it was a myth.

I am as old as metal is, and as I aged the genre aged too. In adulthood, as a doctoral student, academic and writer, I learned that what appears to be metallic hardness is but a patina for something else – the terrifying realisation that, as humans, we are all condemned to the dirt and to the limitations of the body. For all that metal sometimes looks like a playpen for those gripped by delusions of mythic power, at its core there is also fear, despair and brokenness.

It was always there. Hiding in plain sight in Ozzy’s work. Songs like ‘Suicide Solution’ (1980), ‘So Tired’ (1983) and ‘Mama, I’m Coming Home’ (1991) helped to make metal the sound of suffering, and of weakness. That’s true even for metal men who present outwardly as the epitome of the metal warrior. Many of the artists who played Ozzy’s farewell show had explored this territory: Metallica’s ‘Welcome Home (Sanitarium)’ (1986), Pantera’s ‘I’m Broken’ (1994), and Tool’s ‘Forty Six and 2’ (1997) burn with pain and rage.

As a scholar, I learn fast. As a person with a body and a propensity for shame and anxiety, I learn achingly slowly. I wish that, years earlier, I’d internalised what I’d learned metal could be. Like Ozzy, I too have a body that fails me on occasion (I’ve had chronic fatigue syndrome for more than 30 years). Even before that, I never much liked my gawky, ungainly body anyway: I loved metal, but felt I couldn’t be metal. I wrote about the softness at the core of the metal body long before I accepted the squishiness in my own metal bone locker. Yet like Ozzy, I was more metal than I ever could have imagined.

Something had begun to shift for me in the years preceding Ozzy’s final concert. For this male Jewish weakling, metal and shame were natural bedfellows. My children were raised to be shameless: their musical tastes and their frailties were matters of fact. They both found their way to metal with little help from me.

Metal has become the place where my body can betray me, where I can be weak

My daughter fell particularly hard for metallic art. As an autistic person, she knows about limits and excess – meat and drink to metal culture. For years now, I’ve been taking her to gigs. Most recently, as she suffered through an energy-limiting conditions in her late teens, I’ve wheeled her into the disabled section at multiple venues. Unlike Ozzy and unlike me, she was unembarrassed about sitting down. She knew that metal was an ode sung by and to and about fallible bodies. She knew she was metal.

If only Ozzy had known that, too. He knew only the contrast between what he had once tried to be and what he now was: that the monumental myth had crumbled. And I, caught between my daughter’s generation and Ozzy’s, wept tears of sadness for what he would never understand – and tears of happiness for my children’s lack of shame (mingling with tears of pain as my ankle throbbed).

I always thought I would move on from metal as I aged. The opposite happened: following my daughter’s example, metal has become the place where my body can betray me, where I can be weak, where I can acknowledge my frailty. Looking round the audience at gigs, I can see that I am not the only one who knows this.

Ozzy died just 17 days after his final concert, on 22 July 2025. This time I didn’t cry. When I heard the news, I thought ‘How perfect!’ To end one’s life this way, after a mega performance of loving and being loved, was a beautiful thing. For one night only, Ozzy became the one who could strip bare my defences and make me feel. And what a blessing it was to be immobile at the time, joining my dad, my daughter and Ozzy in that place where there is no hiding from the fact that flesh is weak.

item.title: Maxxing treats life as a problem when it’s a mystery
item.dc:creator: Håkon Evjemo
item.description:
The philosopher Gabriel Marcel offers the antidote to a grotesque new ideology: don’t fix existence, be open to it

- by Håkon Evjemo

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
In 2021, while working from home at my corporate law gig, I became obsessed with napping. Throughout my working life, the post-lunch slump felt like an unavoidable feature of the 9-to-5. Then I read Why We Sleep (2017) by Matthew Walker. It was one of a new breed of popular books that used scientific research to deepen our understanding of everyday activities. This book did two things for me. First, it justified my post-lunch nap as a way of optimising my afternoons. Second, and more importantly, it transformed what I considered to be an unavoidable feature of life into a fixable bug. Going beyond the science of sleep, it presented me with the taste of a new approach to life, one that could, if taken to the extreme, conceivably reduce my life to a series of problems amenable to practicable solutions.

Equipped with this newfound confidence in the power of solving life’s problems, I went on a reading spree. I cultivated atomic habits. I learned the Wim Hof Method. Embraced the plasticity of my own brain. Gorged on healthy fats. Cut out gluten. Lined my kitchen with jars of home-made sauerkraut.

Eating well, exercising regularly, learning new skills – these are cornerstones of many self-improvement regimes. Who would not welcome a bit of science to shed more light on how these work? This is precisely what books like Why We Sleep – as well as Atomic Habits (2018) by James Clear, Mind Your Gut (2024) by Kate Scarlata and Megan Riehl, and The Brain that Changes Itself (2007) by Norman Doidge – intend. And yet, working my way through these books I could not help but notice something more nefarious at play. This new toolkit of science-backed interventions seemed to grow into something greater than the sum of their parts. The question of the good life was devolving into a far less ambitious task: the solved life. When we fully reduce life to a series of problems in need of solutions, and when we rely exclusively on these solutions as the means to live a good life, we have succumbed to what I call the scientification of the good life.

Where might the scientification of the good life lead us? In recent years, this relatively innocuous application of science to life has curdled into something grotesque. We are now in an era of what Gen Z calls ‘maxxing’: internet slang for ruthlessly quantifying and optimising social or physiological traits in pursuit of better social standing or lifestyle. The most notable figure is Clavicular (real name Braden Eric Peters), the figurehead of ‘looksmaxxing’, a sub-genre of maxxing that urges people, usually young men, to optimise their physical proportions and facial structure to meet ideal standards. The purpose of looksmaxxing is to ‘mog’, or dominate other men by being more attractive. Common interventions include smashing the jawbone to achieve facial symmetry, self-prescribed methamphetamine to manage weight, and the injection of peptides for supposed skincare benefits.

Looksmaxxing only scratches the surface of a subculture evolving into a full-blown ideology, complete with its own market, language and devoted followers. The proliferation of other forms of maxxing – sleepmaxxing, statusmaxxing, financemaxxing, even vibemaxxing – signals its tendency to expand beyond addressing one particular aspect of life to addressing life as a whole. What fundamentally motivates maxxing is the need to take control by forcefully reducing life to a series of fixable problems. While pseudoscientific interventions like bonesmashing and mewing have taken the ‘science’ out of scientification, the underlying problem-solving attitude I got a taste of has not only remained but has been, as it were, put on steroids, bringing with it the overinflated expectation of actually solving life. Has maxxing delivered on its promises? All I have seen is an obsession with hollow values that lead to substance abuse, infertility, even incarceration. Clearly something profound is missing from the maxxing lifestyle.

If there was any figure I would nominate as a fantasy guest on a maxxer’s livestream or podcast, it would be the 20th-century Catholic existentialist Gabriel Marcel. Though born in 1889, his work reads almost like a philosophical diagnosis of the maxxing trend. Marcel mixed existentialism and phenomenology to cultivate a style of philosophising that relied on common language and everyday experience. His central preoccupation was the ‘ontological mystery’: how to remain open to existence as something we inhabit, rather than a problem to fix. His main warning to maxxers would be this: stop trying to reduce life to a series of problems in need of a fix. Learn to live it.

Hospitals, once understood as places of care, attentiveness and solidarity in the face of suffering, become repair shops

In The Philosophy of Existentialism (1956), Marcel offers a critique of modernity. It begins with a simple observation: the modern world appears broken in the way a machine appears broken. Science affords us the ability to understand how something works, to set standards of ideal function, and therefore to know when things fall short. Brokenness becomes an essential feature of this world. For Marcel, this tendency to see the world as broken eventually turns inward. We come to see ourselves as nothing more than an ‘agglomeration of functions’ (physiological, social, even economic) that adhere to scientifically determined standards amenable to restoration, preservation or enhancement.

This changes the way we approach life. Whether it’s getting your 10,000 steps in a day, cultivating a healthy relationship with your family members, or meeting your KPI’s at work, life becomes governed by what Marcel calls a ‘vital schedule’ designed to repair, regulate, even optimise these functions. Hospitals, once understood as places of care, attentiveness and solidarity in the face of suffering, become repair shops. Workplaces, once sites of vocation, craft and communal purpose, become sites of efficiency. Even my daily naps are tweaks to my own vital schedule. Marcel’s warning is that total immersion in functionality excludes something: ‘this world is, on the one hand, riddled with problems and, on the other, determined to allow no room for mystery.’

According to Marcel, this world of agglomerated functions suffers from a peculiar blindness: it mistakes mysteries for problems. Problems are detachable things we can step back from and solve. Examples include nourishing your gut microbiome after a strong course of antibiotics, navigating toxic relationships, or investing smartly to build your pension. A mystery, by contrast, is what he calls ‘a problem which encroaches upon its own data’: situations in which we are so profoundly implicated that no amount of diagnostic distance can resolve them. Life is one of these mysteries. Matthew Walker can tell me why I am tired. He cannot tell me why, after the nap, I still felt hollow working another lacklustre day drafting commercial property leases for a global pension fund. That hollowness is not a problem to be solved. It is a mystery to be inhabited. And it is precisely this distinction, between the solved life and the lived one, that pop-sci self-helpery, for all its genuine utility, papers over.

For Marcel, whether we treat life as a problem or a mystery depends on whether we adopt the style of ‘having’ or ‘being’. To ‘have’ a life is to treat life as an object I possess. To ‘be’ a life is to recognise I am profoundly implicated in it. This distinction maps onto the difference between problems and mysteries. We ‘have’ problems. A problem is something I can step outside of and inspect from a distance. Its amenability to solution is guaranteed by the fact that I am not implicated in it. It is ‘out there’, waiting to be solved by a method I bring to it. A mystery, by contrast, is something I ‘am’. I cannot step outside of it because I inhabit it, and what I inhabit cannot be diagnosed and solved from a distance. If problem-solving fails in the face of mysteries, I am forced to adopt a different style of living.

Marcel’s key observation is this: ‘having’ is always a temporary excursion from ‘being’. As Marcel puts it in Being and Having (1949), ‘having tends, not to be destroyed, but to be sublimated and changed into being.’ Like dams that break the flow of water, the act of ‘having’ involves what Marcel calls ‘a kind of suppressed dynamic’. I can posit my body as an object for me, then work on it as if it were a broken machine, but I always have to return to my body as something to live in. The dam of ‘having’ my body as something to work on always breaks. This return to being is not incidental but structural: ‘being’ sustains ‘having’, the mystery of living will always encapsulate the solving of problems.

Stop trying to perfect the system of yourself. Instead, cultivate a willingness to be surprised by your own existence

The scientification of the good life overlooks this. It promises a world of pure ‘having’, dictated entirely by diagnosing and solving problems. But the inevitable moments of return, in which the attitude of having and solving problems reverts to the mystery of being, puncture this fantasy. The life that we return to after tweaking it from afar still has to be lived, to be inhabited, and whatever this style of living is, it cannot be served by scientification. For Marcel, the maxxer’s tragedy is not that they are wrong about the value of optimisation, but that they have narrowed their existential horizon exclusively to problem-solving. Instead of trying to fix the mystery of being, maxxers should be finding ways to be at home in it.

This involves not just relinquishing control over what you cannot control, but relinquishing the very attitude of being in control. Admittedly, this is a hard sell, especially for those who believe achieving full control can lead to a good life. This is made harder by the fact that there is no ideal function of participation and therefore is no ‘How to…’ guide on how to participate in life. But to be clear, Marcel doesn’t suggest we abandon all forms of problem-solving. A sleep deficit is a problem; taking a nap solves it. His warning is that life ultimately exceeds the limits of problem-solving. The danger of scientification arises only when we mistake ‘having’ for an exclusive style of living.

Abraham Maslow’s law of the instrument suggests that, to someone with a hammer, everything looks like a nail. Marcel develops this into what we might now call a ‘law of the toolbox’: in a world shaped by techno-scientific success, everything is seen as a problem to be solved. This is an infectious style of living. But this style, effective as it is, becomes self-reinforcing and exclusive of other styles of living. For the maxxers scrolling through morning routines and biohacking protocols, Marcel offers an uncomfortable wisdom: stop trying to perfect the system of yourself. Instead, cultivate a willingness to be surprised by your own existence, to acknowledge what cannot be measured or fixed. This is not passivity. It is a deeper form of engagement. One that recognises the limits of mastery and finds meaning precisely in what escapes our control.

item.title: Go ahead, jump on the bandwagon
item.dc:creator: Hannah Seo
item.description:
Rooting for a team and other collective experiences are opportunities to be seized – even if only once in a while

- by Hannah Seo

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I will confess that, when it comes to sports, I am a fair-weather fan. I like basketball but had little interest in the New York Knicks until they made it to the NBA finals in June. I’m barely interested in soccer unless the Canadian team or the Korean team make it at least to the World Cup round of 32. I root for teams when there’s cause to hope and, when they do advance, I’m as joyful and riotous as any fan.

My intermittent fandom used to be a source of sheepishness. It’s easy to feel, or be made to feel, like a fake fan or a poseur. Especially if you’re among ‘real’, lifelong fans. But this year, I’ve learned to embrace fair-weather fandom as a legitimate way to join in with a collective experience. While there will always be someone out there who might grumble about my fan status or try to flex their superior knowledge of player history, I’ve found that most people are just happy you’re celebrating with them – that you’ve come to recognise a team’s greatness.

Jumping on bandwagons is a normal and valuable part of life, really. We all use cues from the people around us to decide when and where to shift our attention. And if, for a brief window of time, we turn that gaze to a sports team we wouldn’t ordinarily focus on, that’s our prerogative. After all, watching sports can be really good for our psychological wellbeing – in part, research suggests, because of the social connection it promotes as we watch along with other fans. I particularly love those moments when a crowd of like-minded fans grows tense, hearts all racing together, until our team pulls through and we erupt into roars. When there’s an opportunity to participate in that shared drama and excitement, we should seize it.

item.title: A brief history of Viagra
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Discovered by accident, it became the fastest-selling drug of the century. Did it revolutionise sex or reinforce old ideas?

- Video by BBC Ideas, The Open University

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: In the 1990s, an otherwise unremarkable trial for a potential angina treatment ushered in a new chapter in the history of sex and sexuality. The discovery of some unexpected side effects resulted in the widespread availability of sildenafil – better known by its brand name, Viagra. In this animation, delivered with a healthy dose of bawdy humour, the UK sex educator Justin Hancock offers a brief history of the drug, which provided an effective and relatively cheap solution to the age-old issue of erectile disfunction. Further, Hancock considers the pitfalls of the little blue pill, including the concern that other potential uses of sildenafil have been under-studied and sidelined, and that it’s boosted some unhelpful ideas about sex and masculinity.

item.title: Terminal lucidity: when dying dementia patients regain awareness
item.dc:creator: Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston
item.description:
The reports span centuries and cultures. If they’re real, memory and identity might be far more recoverable than we thought

- by Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
An 81-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer’s is living in a retirement home in Iceland. She hasn’t recognised her family or spoken a word to them in a year. One day, while her son Lydur is sitting beside her working on a crossword puzzle, she sits up and looks him directly in the face.

‘My Lydur,’ she says. ‘I am going to recite a verse to you.’

And then she says the following in a loud and clear voice:

Oh, father of light, be adored.
Life and health you gave to me,
My father and my mother.
Now I sit up, for the sun is shining.
You send your light in to me.
Oh, God, how good you are.

She then lies back down and never talks again. In a month, she dies.

This case, reported in a 2011 study by the biologist Michael Nahm and colleagues from the University of Virginia and the University of Iceland, is an example of terminal lucidity: an unexpected return of cognitive function in patients with severe dementia (or other brain damage) that occurs shortly before death.

As a neuroscientist, my first thoughts when encountering reports like this are that they can’t possibly be real. The main reason is that, by the time patients with severe dementia die, their brains are catastrophically damaged. For a protracted period before death, these patients typically show no signs of recognising family members. They often haven’t responded meaningfully to their environment in months or years. And they’ve lost 20 to 50 per cent of their synaptic connections – so much that their brains have visibly shrunk on MRI scans.

On top of this existing damage, the dying process itself is hardly optimal for brain function. Everything we know about neuroscience says this should make cognition worse, not better.

And yet, terminal lucidity keeps being reported.

If a dying brain can spontaneously access ‘lost’ memories, perhaps we could induce a living brain to do the same

In some reports, 60 to 70 per cent of dementia caregivers say they’ve witnessed at least one patient return to lucidity in the days before death. In a study that specifically followed deaths in hospice, researchers found examples of terminal lucidity in 6 per cent of cases. That makes the phenomenon neither ubiquitous nor rare – in the US alone, it would mean around 10,000 cases per year.

This potentially has profound implications for neuroscience and medicine.

Retaining memories depends on neural circuitry maintaining specific synaptic connection strengths. As dementia progresses, memory worsens because these neural structures physically deteriorate – synapses disintegrate, neurons die. So when a woman who hasn’t recognised her son in a year suddenly calls him by name and recites a poem she learned during her childhood, where have those memories been physically stored? If the neural substrate we thought was necessary for memory is degraded, but the memories can still be accessed, then either our understanding of memory storage is fundamentally wrong, or there’s some resilient substrate we haven’t identified yet.

Right now, around 60 million people have dementia worldwide, and their care costs more than $1 trillion each year. The newest treatments attempt to remove accumulations of abnormally folded proteins in the brain, known as amyloids, which are believed to contribute to Alzheimer’s. One such treatment is lecanemab (brand name Leqembi), which costs around $30,000 per year, in exchange for, at best, a minuscule reduction in the rate of disease progression (let alone actually reversing the decline).

If terminal lucidity is real, it means that there are naturally occurring conditions under which even severely damaged brains can have their function restored. And if a dying brain can indeed spontaneously access ‘lost’ memories, perhaps we could induce a living brain to do the same.

However, there are good reasons to think terminal lucidity might not be real. Primary among these is observer bias.

Watching a parent slowly lose themselves without ever having a final chance to say goodbye is devastating. People crave the deathbed scenes from books and movies: the elderly relative who pronounces meaningful final words to gathered family before peacefully expiring. But there’s often a long gap between when someone loses the ability to communicate and when they die – days, weeks, months or even years in cases of severe dementia. During this time, family members may rehearse what they wish they could say and dream of what they wish they could hear back, desperately hoping for one last sign, however small, that their loved one recognises them or is trying to communicate.

This creates exactly the conditions for observer bias to flourish.

Consider the case of a 12-year-old girl with cancer, reported in a 2024 study of terminal lucidity among children with severe illnesses. The study, from The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, was made by the paediatric haematologist-oncologist Philip Roehrs in the US and a team of researchers from around the world. They reported that the girl had been unresponsive for months and was eventually declared dead. However, according to her mother, just before the girl died, she had opened her eyes, mouthed ‘I love you’ and ‘I’m ready to go home,’ and blinked her eyes to answer yes/no questions. The researchers added that the mother ‘appeared to consider these moments as signs of life, despite her daughter’s medical condition.’

Reports of terminal lucidity come from emotionally invested family members or caregivers

No one wants to ask a grieving mother about how confident she truly is that her unresponsive daughter briefly regained awareness before dying. But from a scientific perspective: were the words she mouthed meaningful speech or just involuntary muscle movements? The same kind of question applies to a grandmother who seems to smile and nod (postural reflex?) or a dying spouse who squeezes a hand when told ‘I love you’ (muscle spasm?).

This is the problem with nearly all reports of terminal lucidity: they come from emotionally invested family members or caregivers with strong motivations to perceive communication where there might be none. Those witnessing changes in their loved ones often have no scientific training to distinguish meaningful behaviour from reflexes, and no blinding to prevent bias.

In 2024, Joan M Griffin and other researchers surveyed family caregivers who reported witnessing lucid episodes in dementia patients. They found 51 per cent of these episodes involved communication that ‘made complete sense’, with another 32 per cent making ‘some sense’. Though, keep in mind that 48 per cent of episodes occurred at least six months before death, with only 18 per cent happening in the final week. That means that most of these weren’t ‘terminal’ lucid episodes at all – they’re potentially just part of the normal cognitive fluctuations that occur as dementia progresses.

The scientific evidence we currently have for terminal lucidity leaves us almost entirely with anecdotal reports from biased observers, collected retrospectively. These have not been objectively verified and mostly describe ambiguous behaviours that could arguably be explained by wishful interpretation.

So, how can we explain this phenomenon that has been consistently reported across centuries and cultures? Anecdotal reports of patients who haven’t spoken in years suddenly engaging in complex conversation are hard to dismiss as mere muscle spasms or observer bias. Something appears to be going on beyond pure confabulation.

No one has yet published any neuroscientific recording of terminal lucidity as it happens, so we still have no record of what the brain is doing during an episode. Although any explanation is necessarily speculative, we can make educated guesses based on known and related phenomena.

One explanation relates to brain-swelling reduction. Dying patients often develop brain swelling for multiple reasons, such as electrolyte imbalances, low blood protein, kidney or liver failure, inflammation, or damage to the blood-brain barrier. This swelling compresses brain tissue and reduces blood flow, starving neurons of oxygen and glucose. The result is the familiar progression of terminal delirium: confusion, then sleepiness, then coma, then death.

But in their final days, many patients stop eating and drinking entirely. The resulting dehydration could reduce brain swelling, allowing blood flow to increase, which could temporarily restore some cognitive function – a brief window of lucidity before the dying process continues. It’s a simple mechanism: lower intracranial pressure means better movement of blood through the brain, which means more oxygen and glucose in the brain, which in turn means more functional neurons.

Maybe damaged neural networks can spontaneously reorganise in ways that temporarily restore function

Another explanation, perhaps working in tandem with brain-swelling reduction, relates to how brain networks respond to extreme conditions.

Normal consciousness requires a precise balance of neurochemicals. What is referred to as ‘wakefulness’ – the daily state when you are conscious and your brain is actively responding to the world – depends on brainstem neurons continuously releasing neuromodulators like acetylcholine, noradrenaline and histamine into the cortex. When this system breaks down in a damaged or dying brain, people typically become progressively less responsive.

But sometimes, perturbing a broken system can temporarily fix it. If you’ve ever fixed a glitchy electronic device by hitting it, you’ve seen how pushing a malfunctioning system into an unusual state can accidentally restore function.

Maybe something similar happens in dying brains, where under extreme or unusual conditions, damaged neural networks can spontaneously reorganise in ways that temporarily restore function. One research paper speculates that dying brains might generate ‘spontaneous network integration manifesting as lucid behaviour’ through ‘rapid and nonlinear synchronisation’. Translated from Academic into English, this means something like: ‘Weird things might happen in a dying brain that briefly improve function, but we don’t really know what those things are.’

Even after reading many of the studies about terminal lucidity, I genuinely don’t know whether it really exists. Given this, the appropriate response is neither to credulously accept every report nor to entirely dismiss the phenomenon either. Instead, we need to begin studying terminal lucidity properly. For a long time, almost no one was, though that’s beginning to change.

In 2019, the US National Institute on Aging funded a wave of research, and results are arriving. The most important so far, by a team from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, has captured potential lucid episodes on video. Across 1,433 hours of footage from 20 hospice patients, the team identified nine lucid episodes in three participants – events where communication and social engagement spiked far above each patient’s measured baseline. One man, after a two-week decline, spoke in full sentences for two days, named his family members, said ‘I’m leaving soon,’ and died days later.

This isn’t definitive proof that terminal lucidity is real – the study still suffered from potential observer bias. But it’s the best evidence so far that something is happening that can’t be waved away as grief-soaked confabulation.

What we still don’t have is any evidence of physiological changes during terminal lucidity. There have been no brain scans during an episode, nor blood work to accompany them. A group of researchers at New York University Langone Health, led by Sam Parnia, has been planning continuous EEG monitoring of 500 dying dementia patients, which might someday tell us what brain activity looks like during lucid episodes.

If the video evidence holds up, and if some future study finds a physiological signature to match that evidence, the picture of dementia we currently have would need rethinking. Memory and identity would need to be understood as more distributed, more redundant, and more recoverable than the standard neurodegenerative story allows. And instead of pouring billions into another hopeless amyloid-clearing drug, we might finally have a treatment path worth pursuing – if only we can discover how to stretch a lucid episode into a lasting return.

item.title: Say yes to regret
item.dc:creator: Sandra Lamb
item.description:
After my husband died, I fell into a dark ruminative spiral. The way back would begin at 2pm tomorrow

- by Sandra Lamb

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
The phone rang five times, and then it rang some more. I was calling from Charlotte, North Carolina – wedged into the cracked-leather passenger seat of a friend’s Honda, my suitcase still exhaling the recycled-air odour of the airport – trying to reach Charles at home in Denver. It was eight in the morning in Denver, long past the time he’d normally be stirring raisins into his oatmeal, waiting for his toast to brown.

Six rings. Seven. Eight. Each one twisted something in my chest.

We’d had words that morning as he drove me to the airport – one of those marital skirmishes that feels urgent and forgettable at the same time, but leaves a residue.

On the 10th ring, there was a clatter – the sound of the receiver being knocked, fumbled, dragged across the nightstand. Then Charles’s voice, dry as autumn leaves: ‘Hello.’

Even through the phone line, I could hear the sleep thick in his throat. I apologised for waking him.

‘I need to cancel my appointment this morning,’ he rasped.

‘Don’t worry,’ I countered. ‘I’ll call. Just go back to sleep.’

I told him I loved him, hoping he heard an apology tucked inside those three syllables – a white flag folded and slipped between the words – for my role in the dustup. He said something I couldn’t quite make out. Then the line went dead.

Charles was having three kinds of days then: good days, not-so-good days, and what he called ‘soldiering on’ days. I couldn’t tell which this was, but he was fine when I left, and we’d agreed I should make this trip. We’d bought tickets to California for the following weekend – relatives in Lodi expecting us.
